en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Bhojanavagga 35.
The Training Rule on the Invitation Ceremony (Pavāraṇā-sikkhāpada).
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain brahmin invited some bhikkhus and fed them.
After the bhikkhus had finished eating and were satisfied, they went to their relatives' homes; some ate there, while others took almsfood and departed.
Then that brahmin said this to his neighbors:
“Venerable sirs, I have satisfied the bhikkhus.
Come, I shall satisfy you as well.
They replied, “How will you satisfy us, venerable sir?”
“Those who were invited by you also came to our houses; some ate there, while others took their alms-food and departed.
Then that brahmin complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying, “How can these venerable ones, having eaten in our house, go to eat elsewhere?”
"And I am not capable of giving as much as you require.
The monks heard that brahmin complaining, grumbling, and lamenting.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before]... they complained, grumbled, and lamented:
“How can these monks, having finished their meal and being invited to stop, eat elsewhere? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, monks, that monks, having finished their meal and being invited to stop, eat elsewhere?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can those foolish men, monks, having finished their meal and been invited to stop, eat otherwise?
This, monks, is neither for the inspiration of the unconfident nor for the increase of the confident…” [and so on].
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whosoever monk, having finished his meal and being invited to eat more, should chew or consume solid or soft food, it is an offense entailing expiation.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, the monks were bringing choice almsfood out for the sick monks.
The sick ones did not eat it to their heart's content,
and the other monks threw it away.
The Blessed One heard a loud noise, a great clamor, like the cawing of crows.
Having heard it, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, what is this loud noise, this great clamor, like the cawing of crows?”
Then the Venerable Ānanda reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“But, Ānanda, may the bhikkhus eat what has been left over by one who is ill?
“They may not, Blessed One.”
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this context, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to eat what is left over, whether one is ill or not ill.
And in this way, bhikkhus, it should be made left over:”
‘Enough of all this.
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
“Whichever monk, having finished his meal and being invited to stop, should eat or consume fresh or cooked food that is not left over, it is an offense entailing expiation.”
"But whoever" means whoever such a person... "a monk" means... [as before]... a monk.
... [as before] ... in this context, "bhikkhu" is intended in this sense.
One who has "eaten" (bhuttāvī) is one who has eaten any one of the five kinds of cooked food, even if only as much as the tip of a blade of kusa grass.
"Invited" means that solid food is perceived, soft food is perceived, it is brought while standing within arm's reach, and a refusal is perceived.
"Not left over" means:
It has been made unallowable;
it has been made unaccepted;
it has been made unspoken.
It is done when [the recipient] is outside the reach of one's hand;
it is done by one who has not yet eaten;
it is done by one who has finished eating, has refused further food, and has risen from his seat.
When it has not been said, “Enough of all this,” and it is not leftover from one who is ill—
this is called “not excessive.”
What is called "leftover" (atiritta) is that which has been made permissible (kappiyakata) and that which has been formally accepted (paṭiggahitakata).
It has been performed by one who has spoken;
it has been performed within arm’s reach;
it has been performed by one who has finished eating.
It has been eaten by one who has finished his meal and refused further food;
it has been made allowable by saying, "Enough of all this";
it is the remainder of what was left over for the sick.
This is called "leftover.

As for "hard food," it refers to the five types of cooked food; setting aside those things that may be taken during the watch of the night, those that may be taken for seven days, and those that may be taken for life, the remainder is called "hard food."
“Eatable food” means the five kinds of cooked food: boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, and meat.
If one receives it with the intention, “I will chew it; I will eat it,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one eats or consumes fresh or cooked food when it is not leftover, perceiving it as not leftover, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one eats or consumes fresh or cooked food when it is not leftover, being doubtful about it, there is an offense of expiation.
If one eats or consumes fresh or cooked food when it is not leftover, perceiving it as leftover, there is an offense of expiation.
If one accepts for the purpose of food that which is to be consumed within a watch of the day, within seven days, or for as long as life lasts, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
For every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is a surplus [of food] and one perceives it as not being a surplus, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is more than sufficient and he is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is more than sufficient and he perceives it as more than sufficient, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
He eats after having had it made leftover;
he receives it with the intention, "I will eat it after having had it made leftover";
he goes away taking it for the sake of another.
One who eats the leftovers of the sick;
one who, when there is a reason, consumes what is to be used within a watch of the night, what is to be used for seven days, or what is to be used for as long as life lasts;
one who is insane.
"For the first offender":
thus ends the fifth training rule concerning the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā).
